directAnswer: Vigilius was pope from 537 to 555, one of the most troubled pontificates of late antiquity. Installed after the deposition of Silverius under Byzantine pressure, he spent years in Constantinople during the Three Chapters controversy, reversing his position more than once before accepting the decisions of the Second Council of Constantinople in 553. He died at Syracuse on his way home and is not venerated as a saint.

paras: Vigilius came from a Roman aristocratic family. As a deacon he was briefly named successor by Boniface II, who withdrew the designation, and he later served as papal representative in Constantinople, where he gained the confidence of Empress Theodora.

Writers of the time, including Liberatus and Procopius, report that Theodora backed him in return for a promise to support the deposed Patriarch Anthimus; historians weigh these accounts carefully, as some were hostile. After Belisarius deposed Silverius in March 537, Vigilius was installed as bishop of Rome. Silverius's death later that year removed any rival claim, and Vigilius was recognized by the Roman clergy.

To win over opponents of Chalcedon, Justinian issued an edict around 544 condemning three sets of writings associated with Antiochene theology: the person and works of Theodore of Mopsuestia, certain writings of Theodoret of Cyrus, and a letter of Ibas of Edessa. Western bishops objected that this undermined Chalcedon, which had received Theodoret and Ibas.

In 545 Vigilius was taken from Rome and, after a stay in Sicily, arrived in Constantinople in 547. In 548 he issued a document called the Iudicatum condemning the Three Chapters while affirming Chalcedon. The reaction in the West was severe; a council in Africa broke communion with him, and he withdrew the document.

sections.h2: Conflict with Justinian and the Council of 553
paras: When Justinian published a further condemnation in 551 without waiting for a council, Vigilius protested and took refuge in a church in Constantinople and later in the Church of St. Euphemia at Chalcedon. Accounts say imperial soldiers tried to drag him from the altar.

Justinian convened the Second Council of Constantinople in 553. Vigilius refused to attend and issued a Constitutum that rejected the writings in question but declined to condemn the persons of Theodoret and Ibas. The council condemned the Three Chapters and removed his name from the diptychs. Isolated and in poor health, he accepted the council's decisions in documents issued in December 553 and February 554.

With Justinian's permission to return, Vigilius obtained from the emperor the Pragmatic Sanction of 554, which regulated the government of reconquered Italy. He set out for Rome but died at Syracuse in Sicily on June 7, 555. His body was brought to Rome and buried in the church of San Marcello on the Via Salaria.

His acceptance of the council was rejected for decades by churches in northern Italy, leading to a lasting schism centered on Aquileia. Vigilius's career is often studied as an example of the pressures placed on the papacy by Byzantine emperors.

keyFacts: Pope from 537 to 555, installed after the deposition of Silverius
Spent roughly eight years in Constantinople during the Three Chapters controversy
Issued the Iudicatum (548), later withdrew it, then accepted the 553 council
Pope during the Second Council of Constantinople (553)
Died at Syracuse in 555; not venerated as a saint

faqs.question: What was the Three Chapters controversy?
faqs.answer: It was a dispute over Justinian's condemnation of writings by Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrus, and Ibas of Edessa. Many Western bishops feared this weakened the Council of Chalcedon.

faqs.question: Did Pope Vigilius attend the Second Council of Constantinople?
faqs.answer: No. He was in Constantinople but refused to attend. He later accepted the council's condemnation of the Three Chapters in 553 and 554.

faqs.question: Why did Pope Vigilius change his position so often?
faqs.answer: He was caught between Justinian's pressure in Constantinople and strong Western opposition to condemning the Three Chapters. He tried to protect Chalcedon's authority while dealing with an emperor who controlled his movements.
